I am 65 years old and have worked these fields in Quzhou County for more than forty years. I finished middle school, which gave me enough schooling to read labels and keep basic accounts, but the real knowledge came from my father and from watching the seasons change year after year. My household has about 10 mu of land, and like most of my neighbors I follow the wheat-maize double-cropping system that has fed our families for generations. The winter wheat went into the ground last October before the hard frost, and now that spring has arrived the crop is greening up and I am already planning the first irrigation and top-dressing. I will keep 8 mu in the wheat-maize rotation this year. For wheat I use improved varieties—some years I save my own seed and some years I buy fresh certified seed from the township store to keep vigor up, but I never use old traditional landraces anymore because the improved types yield better and resist lodging. For summer maize I always buy hybrid seed; everyone in the village knows that saved maize seed loses half its yield. I rotary-till the wheat ground before sowing, apply compound fertilizer as a basal dose, and then top-dress with urea at green-up and again at jointing. Wheat needs four irrigations—green-up, jointing, heading, and grain-filling—because our spring rains are unreliable. After the wheat comes off in early June I will sow maize directly into the wheat stubble without tillage; no-tillage saves diesel, preserves soil moisture, and lets me plant quickly before the summer heat arrives. Maize only needs two irrigations, one when the plants are knee-high and another at tasseling, assuming the summer monsoon does its job. I spray pesticides four times on wheat and three times on maize, mostly for weeds, aphids, and the fungal diseases that come with our humid July weather. If the season is normal I expect about 500 kg per mu from the wheat and 550 kg per mu from the maize, which is what I and my neighbors usually achieve.
